prize_parts.citation: For empirical evidence on how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality.

statement.case_for: The work shows credibly how trade exposure and technology change labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality. It rests on transparent quasi-experimental designs that have been replicated, challenged and refined for more than a decade, and it changed both the research agenda and the policy debate on globalisation and adjustment costs. On attribution I now prefer Autor, Dorn and Hanson to my opening trio with Katz. The China-shock programme is jointly theirs, and that is the most specific and defensible credit on this ballot item. Compared with my opening first choice, B018, the credit here is much less diffuse. B018 asks the Committee to pick three from at least eight strong contributors, and that choice is the weakest part of its case. I have moved B036 up on that attribution ground, not because of the opening counts.
statement.case_against: The size and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the shift-share identification behind them, are still debated. The ballot item bundles two strands, task-based or skill-biased technical change and the trade-shock evidence, and a three-person prize centred on the trade shock leaves part of the technology and task lineage uncredited (Katz, and Acemoglu, who was recognised in 2024). The labour prizes of 2021 and 2023 and the 2024 technology and institutions prize also overlap thematically. A reasonable member could conclude that the combined item is not yet a single, cleanly framed discovery.

responses.point: The China-shock work is clearly credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Katz's core contribution sits close to lineage already recognised through the Goldin prize, and the task-based and trade-shock strands are distinct and hard to bundle.
responses.response: I agree on attribution, and it changes my proposal. In my opening I named Katz in place of Dorn. His skill-premium work is foundational, but it is a different strand from the trade-shock evidence, and crediting it would require a citation built around technology and skills. I therefore move to Autor, Dorn and Hanson with a citation on trade and technology exposure. I do not accept that the two strands are too hard to bundle. Autor's own work spans both, and that gives the citation a coherent centre. I accept that Katz and the task lineage go unrecognised under this configuration.

responses.point: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are the core of modern monetary policy analysis, with a defensible core of Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. The work is fully mature, and the 2022 banking prize does not overlap with it.
responses.response: I ranked B018 first and still regard its scientific importance and maturity as very high. What moves me is attribution. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets have claims that a three-name cap cannot accommodate, and post-2008 and post-pandemic experience has qualified how the framework is read. That is why I now keep B018 as an alternative and not as my preferred prize. If the Committee judges the Calvo, Taylor and Woodford core to be clean enough, I would support it. I do not think the question is settled by how many members ranked it first.

responses.point: The China-shock programme is clearly Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The work has had about a decade of replication and critical re-examination, including debate over magnitudes and persistence, and is mature enough for recognition.
responses.response: I agree with the attribution and the maturity judgment. I would qualify one point. Persistence is not a side issue, because it determines whether the contribution is a lasting empirical discovery or a contested estimate. The strongest version of the case is the design and the finding of concentrated local adjustment costs, with the debate over magnitudes presented as part of how the field matured. The citation should therefore be worded around the evidence on exposure and adjustment and should avoid claiming a precise size for the effect.

responses.point: The China-shock core fits three names, but credit for the task framework is split with Acemoglu, who has already won, and the Committee may see overlap with recent technology and growth prizes.
responses.response: That overlap is real, and it is a further reason to centre the citation on the empirical trade and technology exposure evidence and not on the theory of tasks. The theoretical task framework is where Acemoglu's recognition and the recent growth and technology prizes would matter most. The Autor, Dorn and Hanson evidence is a different kind of contribution, so I do not think the overlap defeats the case. It does mean the wording needs care.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee would see the trade-shock evidence and the task and technology literature as one achievement, or would prefer a narrower trade-shock prize or a broader technology and labour prize.
How much weight the debated long-run magnitude and persistence of the China shock should carry in judging lasting discovery.
Whether leaving out Katz, and the task-framework credit shared with Acemoglu, is an acceptable attribution cost.
Whether B018 would be more compelling to the Committee if a clean three-name credit were agreed, which I cannot resolve from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the candidates in the preferred configuration or the alternatives. My ties are to colleagues (SSE affiliation with some committee members) and to market-design collaborators, none of whom appear on these ballot items.
